title: Softmax with cross-entropy
objectives: Derive the gradient of softmax with cross-entropy as the probabilities minus the one-hot target.

screens.title: Scores into chances
screens.prose: A classifier scores three classes with logits $\mathbf{z} = (2, 1, 0.1)$; the true class is 0. To turn scores into chances, exponentiate each and divide by the total: $$p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}.$$ This is the softmax.
screens.question: What is $p_0$? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Exponentiate each logit first, then divide.

byKey.scores: You divided the scores themselves, $2/3.1$. Exponentiate first, so the chances are positive and sum to 1.
byKey.equal: Equal chances ignore the scores. The largest logit should get the most.

explain.text: The softmax gives $(0.659, 0.2424, 0.0986)$: all positive, summing to 1, and in the logits’ order.

screens.title: What moves the chances

screens.title: The loss
screens.prose: Cross-entropy with a one-hot target, from the information theory course, charges $L = -\ln p_y$: the surprise of the true class under the model, in nats because we use $\ln$. Here $y = 0$.
screens.question: What is $L$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Only the true class’s chance enters.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the natural log of $p_0$ and change the sign.

byKey.bits: You used $\log_2$: 0.602 is the same loss in bits. The code uses `np.log`, so nats.
byKey.log10: You used $\log_{10}$. Cross-entropy here is in nats, so use $\ln$.
byKey.prob: That is $p_0$ itself. The loss is $-\ln p_0$.

explain.text: $L = -\ln 0.659 = 0.417$ nats. A model sure of the right class, $p_0 \to 1$, pays $L \to 0$.

screens.title: The gradient of the loss
screens.prose: We want $\partial L/\partial z_i$ for every class $i$, with $L = -\ln p_y$ and $p$ the softmax of $\mathbf{z}$.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: $L = -\ln \frac{e^{z_y}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} = -z_y + \ln \sum_j e^{z_j}$, since the log of a quotient is a difference.
$\frac{\partial}{\partial z_i}(-z_y) = -[i = y]$: only $z_y$ appears, so this is $-1$ for the true class and 0 otherwise.
$\frac{\partial}{\partial z_i} \ln \sum_j e^{z_j} = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}$, by the chain rule: $(\ln u)^\prime = u^\prime/u$.
That fraction is $p_i$, by the definition of the softmax.
So $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i} = p_i - [i = y]$: the chances minus the one-hot target.
$\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i} = -\frac{1}{p_y}$ for every $i$, from $(\ln p)^\prime = 1/p$.
lines.why: That differentiates in $p_y$, not in $z_i$. Each $z_i$ reaches $L$ through the softmax.

hints.text: The log-sum’s derivative is a softmax entry.

feedback.correct: Split the log, differentiate each piece, and recognise $p_i$: $\partial L/\partial z_i = p_i - [i = y]$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Start by writing $L$ as $-z_y$ plus a log-sum.

byKey.x1: You stopped at $p_y$. The chain rule must carry on through the softmax to each $z_i$.
byKey.left-out: Every line but the $1/p_y$ one belongs.

explain.text: Written as $-z_y + \ln \sum_j e^{z_j}$, the loss has two easy pieces. The log-sum gives $p_i$ and the first piece gives $-1$ at the true class: $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}$.

screens.title: Logits near 1000
screens.prose: In float64, `np.exp(1000)` is `inf`, so a softmax of $(1000, 999, 998.1)$ computed directly is `inf/inf`, which is `nan`. The explore screen showed a fix: subtract the largest logit first, which leaves the chances unchanged.
screens.question: What does the softmax of $(1000, 999, 998.1)$ give after subtracting 1000?

options.why: That is the direct route. After subtracting, the largest exponent is $e^0 = 1$, which is safe.
The largest does not take everything: the gaps of 1 and 1.9 still matter.
The logits are not equal: their gaps are those of $(2, 1, 0.1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract 1000 and compare with the course logits.

explain.text: After the shift the exponents are at most $e^0 = 1$, so nothing overflows and the chances equal the course ones. The loss uses the same trick: $\ln \sum_j e^{z_j} = m + \ln \sum_j e^{z_j - m}$, the log-sum-exp form.

screens.title: A batch of rows
screens.prose: Training uses a batch: logits $\mathbf{Z}$ of shape $(n, K)$ and one true class per row. The loss is the average over rows, $L = \tfrac1n \sum_r -\ln p_{r, y_r}$, so each row’s gradient is divided by $n$. Take $n = 2$, with row 1 the course logits.
screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial Z_{1,0}$, row 1, class 0? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The loss is a mean over the 2 rows.

feedback.correct: Row 1’s $p - y$ entry is $-0.341$, divided by $n = 2$: $-0.1705$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The average over 2 rows divides each row’s gradient by 2.

byKey.no-n: You forgot to divide by the batch size. The loss is a mean over 2 rows.
byKey.sign: Check the sign: the true class gets $p - 1$, negative.

explain.text: Each row contributes $\tfrac1n(\mathbf{p}_r - \mathbf{y}_r)$, so the batch gradient is $(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})/n$: $-0.341/2 = -0.1705$ here.

screens.title: tanh and ReLU backwards
screens.prose: Between layers sit elementwise functions. ReLU is $\max(0, z)$: slope 1 where $z > 0$ and 0 where $z < 0$; we take 0 at exactly 0. Backward multiplies the incoming gradient by the slope, entry by entry, as tanh multiplies by $1 - \tanh^2 z$.
screens.question: Fill in the gradient that leaves ReLU.

hints.text: Find the slope of ReLU at each $z$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply each incoming entry by the slope at its $z$.

byKey.no-mask: At $z = -1.5$ ReLU is flat, so nothing passes back.
byKey.at-zero: At exactly $z = 0$ we take slope 0, so nothing passes.
byKey.sign: The slope at $z = 2$ is 1, so the $-0.2$ passes unchanged.

explain.text: ReLU passes $g$ where $z > 0$ and blocks it elsewhere: $(0, 0, -0.2)$. tanh would scale each entry instead, giving $(0.0723, 0.3, -0.0141)$.

screens.title: Softmax, then log
screens.prose: Priya computes the loss in two steps, `-np.log(softmax(z)[y])`, for $\mathbf{z} = (0, -800)$ and $y = 1$. In float64, $e^{-800}$ is below the smallest positive number, so it becomes 0.
screens.question: What does she get, and what is the true loss?

options.why: The two-step route takes the log of a chance that has already underflowed to 0.
The fused form never takes the log of 0, and gives a finite 800.
An unlikely true class costs a lot, not nothing: $-\ln p$ is large when $p$ is small.

feedback.correct: $p_1$ rounds to 0 and $-\ln 0 = \infty$. Fused, $L = \ln \sum_j e^{z_j} - z_1 = 0 - (-800) = 800$, with no small number ever formed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What is $e^{-800}$ in float64?

byKey.b: You assumed the two routes agree. They do on paper; in float64 the chance underflows before the log.

explain.text: Computing the chance first loses it to underflow, and the log of 0 is infinite. The log-sum-exp form works with $z_y$ directly, so $L = 800$; `cross_entropy` must use it.

screens.prose: Write `softmax_ce(logits, targets)` for a batch: `logits` is an $(n, K)$ array and `targets` holds $n$ class indices. Return the mean loss in nats, by log-sum-exp, and the gradient `dlogits`, which is $(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})/n$.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def softmax_ce(logits, targets):
    n = logits.shape[0]
    rows = np.arange(n)
    m = logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(logits - m)
    s = e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    loss = np.mean(m[:, 0] + np.log(s[:, 0]) - logits[rows, targets])
    d = e / s
    d[rows, targets] -= 1
    return loss, d / n
widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests. Each compares the loss and the gradient rounded to 6 places. The cases: the course logits, three seeded rows, logits near 1000, logits $(0, -800)$, and equal logits over 27 classes. One more checks against central differences, and one batch has rows 1000 apart.
widget.postlude:
def matches_differences():
    r = np.random.default_rng(8)
    Z, y = r.standard_normal((4, 5)) * 3, [4, 0, 2, 2]
    _, d = softmax_ce(Z.copy(), y)
    worst, top = 0.0, 1e-12
    for i in np.ndindex(Z.shape):
        up, dn = Z.copy(), Z.copy()
        up[i] += 1e-5
        dn[i] -= 1e-5
        num = (softmax_ce(up, y)[0] - softmax_ce(dn, y)[0]) / 2e-5
        worst = max(worst, abs(d[i] - num))
        top = max(top, abs(d[i]), abs(num))
    return bool(worst / top < 1e-6)

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def softmax_ce(logits, targets):
    n = logits.shape[0]
    rows = np.arange(n)
    m = np.full((n, 1), logits.max())
    e = np.exp(logits - m)
    s = e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    loss = np.mean(m[:, 0] + np.log(s[:, 0]) - logits[rows, targets])
    d = e / s
    d[rows, targets] -= 1
    return loss, d / n
mutants.symptom: One maximum for the whole batch: a row far below the largest logit underflows to zero and the loss is infinite.

screens.title: Next-day return buckets
screens.prose: A desk trains a classifier of tomorrow’s return bucket (down, flat, up) with this loss. For one day it gives chances $(0.2, 0.5, 0.3)$, and the stock went up.
screens.question: What is $\partial L/\partial z_{\text{up}}$ for that day? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}$ with $\mathbf{y}$ one-hot at up.

byKey.no-minus-one: You left out the target: the realised bucket gets $p - 1$.

explain.text: The step raises the up logit (gradient $-0.7$) and lowers the others in proportion to their chances: flat, at 0.5, is pushed down hardest.

ideas: Softmax turns logits into chances, $p_i = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$; adding one number to every logit changes nothing, so subtract the largest first.
With cross-entropy $L = -\ln p_y$ (nats), the gradient is $\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}$: raise the true logit, lower the others by their chances. Over a batch, divide by $n$.
Compute the loss fused, as $\ln \sum_j e^{z_j} - z_y$ with the largest logit taken out: softmax then log underflows to $\ln 0$.

formula.name: Softmax with cross-entropy
formula.note: For $L = -\ln p_y$ on one row; over a batch of $n$ rows, divide by $n$.

summary.trap: Softmax then log turns a tiny chance into $\ln 0$; the fused log-sum-exp form gives the true, finite loss.

quiz.prose: A character model starts with all 27 logits equal: every letter and the end mark alike.
quiz.question: What is its loss on any character, in nats? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Equal logits give $p = \tfrac{1}{27}$ each, so $L = \ln 27 = 3.2958$ nats.
feedback.generic: Not quite. With equal logits each chance is $1/27$.

byKey.bits: That is $\log_2 27$, the same loss in bits.
byKey.prob: That is the chance $1/27$. The loss is $-\ln$ of it.

explain.text: All chances are $\tfrac{1}{27}$, so $L = -\ln \tfrac{1}{27} = \ln 27 = 3.2958$: the loss of knowing nothing, the bar the makemore course starts from.

quiz.question: What is wrong?

options.text: The loss is a mean, so divide the gradient by 4

options.why: That is the rule for one row. The mean adds a factor $\tfrac1n$.

options.text: It should be divided by the 27 classes
options.why: The mean runs over rows, not classes.
Averaging shrinks each row’s share; it does not grow it.

feedback.correct: $L = \tfrac14 \sum_r L_r$, so each row’s gradient carries $\tfrac14$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. How was the loss combined over rows?

explain.text: The batch loss averages 4 rows, so the gradient is $(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Y})/4$. Left undivided, the step is 4 times too large.
